newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK, Washington investigate U.S. immigration officer.
newsitem.headline: HK, Washington investigate U.S. immigration officer.

text.p: U.S. and Hong Kong's authorities are investigating a senior U.S. immigration official and his wife for suspected corruption and abuse of authority, an official said on Sunday.

A U.S. consulate spokesman, Patrick Corcoran, told Reuters those being probed were James DeBates, acting chief of the U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service office in Hong Kong, and his wife Heddy.
Local news media say mainland Chinese are alleged to have obtained U.S. visas by bribery.
DeBates is on "administrative leave" in the United States. Heddy DeBates said the couple had no objection to being investigated.
"Yes, that's OK. They can investigate. No problem... I really don't know what to tell you because you know (if) they want to investigate they can investigate," she said by telephone.
Corcoran said the couple were being investigated by Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) and the Office of the Inspector General of the U.S. Justice Department.

The ICAC said it and the U.S. authority were jointly investigating allegations of corruption and abuse of authority by a Hong Kong-based U.S. Immigration and Naturalization Service official and his wife. The ICAC statement did not name the people involved.
"The enquiries, which are still continuing, are conducted with the full knowledge and co-operation of the U.S. Consulate General in Hong Kong," it said, without giving further details.
Last July, another U.S. immigration officer, Jerry Stuchiner, was arrested by the ICAC in conjunction with U.S. Justice Department officials investigating illegal immigration.
He later received a 40-month jail sentence for possessing forged passports of Honduras, where he had worked for the U.S. Immigration Service.
Illegal immigration from Asia, including China, into the United States had long been a concern for Washington. Some smuggling networks have involved Hong Kong and its people.

Hundreds of mainland Chinese are believed to have sneaked into the U.S. over the past few years with visas obtained through the American immigration office in the territory, local radio quoted unidentified sources as saying.
Bribes are believed to have been received in the past few years in return for helping applicants, mostly mainland Chinese, obtain U.S. visas, the radio said.
